narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Alegrías originated in Cádiz, likely derived from the Aragonese jota during the French occupation.
Enrique Butrón is credited with fixing the current flamenco style, while Ignacio Espeleta introduced the signature 'tiriti, tran, tran' refrain.
on_screen: Map: Spain · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally a festive dance, it is now performed in professional settings and at the annual National Competition of Alegrías in Cádiz.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: File:La Argentinita - Alegrias (ca. 1935).webm (https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8b/La_Argentinita_-_Alegrias_%28ca._1935%29.webm?utm_source=commons.wikimedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=original)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance follows a 12-beat cycle with emphasis on beats 3, 6, 8, 10, and 12.
It requires a sequence of specific sections: salida, paseo, silencio, castellana, zapateado, and bulerías.
Technique involves fluid arm movements, soft footwork, and precise zapateado.
Watch for Zapateado, Silencio.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (gvnf-Kor754)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo performance space
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Alegrías belongs to the cantiñas group, characterized by a festive, major-key melody.
It is played at 120-170 bpm.
Listen for the Flamenco guitar, Voice.
The pulse is 12-beat cycle at about 145 beats a minute.
A lively, major-key flamenco form characterized by rapid rhythmic cycles and expressive, elaborate vocal lines.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear ankle-length dresses with ruffles, often with a bata de cola.
Accessories include mantillas, flowers, combs, and coral earrings.
High-heeled shoes are essential for the zapateado.

Alegrías de Córdoba, which features shifts between major and minor keys.
